newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Wheat prices soar as freeze hits young U.S. crop.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Wheat prices soar as freeze hits young U.S. crop.

text.p: Wheat prices soared on Monday after freezing temperatures clamped down on the developing winter wheat crop in the United States, threatening to cut both production and exports this year, analysts said.

Charlie Sernatinger, director of commodity operations at trading house Man International, estimated that up 150 million bushels, or four million metric tons, of wheat were lost when freezing temperatures swept from Kansas to Texas.
"This is two million tons of exportable wheat we cannot afford to lose," he said, referring to the portion of the damaged crop that would likely have been sold overseas.

"Wheat is sometimes compared to a cat with nine lives," said Al Peterlin, chief meteorologist of the U.S. Agriculture Department. "This cat fell off a cliff and we're trying to see how many of the nine lives were used up. There's no question we have done some damage and caused some stress to the plants."

That message was not lost on futures traders, who just over a year ago sent wheat prices to a record high of $7.50 a bushel on similar worries about the U.S. crop. At that time, world grain stocks were at 20-year lows.

On Monday, wheat for May delivery at the Chicago Board of Trade jumped the 20-cent-per-bushel daily trading limit at the opening bell and stayed there. May wheat closed at $4.23, up 20 cents and the highest closing price since September 3.
At the Kansas City Board of Trade, May wheat also ended up the daily limit of 25 cents a bushel at $4.76-1/2.
The speculative buying in wheat spilled over to other grains, with corn for May delivery closing up 4-1/4 cents a bushel at $3.03-3/4 and May soybeans up 2-1/2 cents at $8.33.
The grain rally helped push commodity indexes to higher closes, with the Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures prices ending at 244.66 points, up 1.95.

Temperatures dipped into the teens Fahrenheit over the weekend from Kansas into Oklahoma and the Texas panhandle, where winter wheat planted last fall has been emerging from dormancy to start forming new leaves.
Joel Burgio, a meteorologist with Weather Services Corp, said, "The damage occurred on Saturday and Sunday. We had a very serious freeze on those two mornings."
Rollie Sears, a Kansas State University wheat breeder, estimated a 40 percent production loss in southern Kansas, an area that produced 40 percent of the state's wheat last year.
Kansas alone produces 10 to 20 percent of the annual U.S. wheat crop of about 2.3 billion bushels.
"We had a good crop, and basically the potential for a good crop is out the window," Sears said. "Right now it is pretty depressing."

As the freeze hit, world wheat supplies remained tight. The U.S. Agriculture Department on April 11 estimated world wheat stocks at 108.3 million metric tons by July, down from 112.2 million estimated a month earlier.
Recent dry weather has also reduced crop prospects for Australia and France, two of the top five wheat exporters.
Meanwhile, world wheat consumption is expected to rise to 579 million tons this year from 552 million a year ago.

With Monday's gains, wheat prices have risen 14 percent since April 4. Traders were already worried about flooding in the Dakotas and Minnesota, the heart of the U.S. spring wheat belt which is now bound to see planting delays.
Acreage planted to hard red winter wheat from Kansas to Texas was already down five percent this year at 34.1 million acres as many farmers planned on planting high-priced crops like soybeans.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices ended higher on a report linking Iran, the third largest oil exporter, to the 1996 bombing of a U.S. military compound in Saudi Arabia. The report came at time when diplomatic tensions are already high between the West and Iran.
The Washington Post on Sunday reported that U.S. and Saudi intelligence authorities had linked a senior Iranian government official to a group suspected of bombing the facility.

In Tehran, meanwhile, several hundred students clased with police outside the German embassy during a demonstration against last week's Berlin court ruling that Iran ordered the killing of dissidents.

"The report linking Iran to the bombing set the stage for further gains today when tensions were already mounting since Thursday with the Germany-Iran situation," said Richard Redash, analyst with Prudential Securities.
Crude oil deliverable in May ended 37 cents a barrel higher at $19.90. May unleaded gasoline closed up 1.08 cents at 61.96 cents a gallon and May heating oil up 0.80 cent at 54.67 cents gallon.
